directAnswer: Pope Leo VIII was a Roman layman elected in 963 at the synod that Otto I convened to depose John XII. His pontificate was contested until Benedict V's deposition in June 964, and the modern Church counts him as legitimate from that point until his death in 965.

paras: Leo was a senior official of the papal administration, holding the post of protoscriniarius, head of the chancery's scribes, but he was not a cleric. After Otto's synod declared John XII deposed in December 963, it chose Leo, and he received all the clerical orders within a very short time before being consecrated. Such rapid elevation violated church norms and fueled opposition to him.

When Otto left Rome in early 964, the Romans rose against Leo, and he fled to the emperor. John XII returned and condemned him. After John's death the Romans elected Benedict V, but Otto besieged the city, restored Leo, and had Benedict deposed in June 964. From then until his death on 1 March 965, Leo reigned without a rival.

Several documents attributed to Leo VIII grant the emperor sweeping rights, including control over papal elections and the investiture of bishops. Historians recognize these as forgeries produced during the eleventh-century Investiture Controversy. Leo's actual surviving acts are few, and his reign is best understood as a product of imperial politics.

keyFacts: Elected December 963; counted as legitimate pope from 23 June 964 to 1 March 965
A layman and papal official (protoscriniarius) before election
Received all clerical orders in rapid succession
Restored by Otto I after the deposition of Benedict V
Imperial privileges bearing his name are later forgeries

faqs.question: Why is Leo VIII's legitimacy debated?
faqs.answer: He was elected while John XII was still alive, through a deposition of questionable validity. The Church counts him as pope only after Benedict V's deposition in 964.

faqs.question: Did Leo VIII give the emperor control over papal elections?
faqs.answer: Documents claiming so exist, but they are later forgeries from the Investiture Controversy, not genuine acts of Leo.
